config.title: Find Peak Element

intro.title: Find Peak Element
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that finds a 'peak element' in an array. A peak element is an element that is greater than or equal to its immediate neighbors. You will learn to implement a binary search algorithm to solve this lesson efficiently. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays, conditional logic, and loop constructs. By the end, you will understand how to apply binary search to find a peak in O(log n) time.
intro.usecase: The peak finding algorithm is essential in data analysis applications where you need to identify local maximums in datasets. For example, in financial dashboards, analysts use this to spot price peaks in stock charts to inform trading decisions. In weather monitoring systems, it helps identify temperature spikes across geographic sensor data displayed on interactive maps. E-commerce platforms apply similar logic to find sales peaks during promotional periods within their analytics panels.

objectives: Implement a linear search algorithm to find a peak element in an array
Construct a binary search approach to efficiently locate peak elements
Apply edge case handling for arrays with single elements or monotonic sequences
Manipulate array indices to compare neighboring elements during peak detection
Initialize test cases with various array configurations to validate the algorithm
Integrate the peak-finding algorithm into a function that returns the index of any peak
Configure the algorithm to handle both ascending and descending array patterns

content.body: Have you ever looked at a mountain range and tried to spot the highest peak? In programming, we often need to find peaks in arrays. Today, you'll learn how to find a peak element efficiently using a clever memory technique.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply the 'remember what we've seen' mental model to find peaks
• Implement a single-pass solution using a lookup structure
• Explain why checking neighbors is enough to identify a peak
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: Look at this tiny array: [1, 3, 2]. Which element is a peak? (A peak is greater than its neighbors)
content.successMessage: Great! 3 is a peak because it's greater than both neighbors (1 and 2).

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.prompt: Now try [1, 2, 3, 1]. Which element is a peak?
content.successMessage: Perfect! 3 is a peak because it's greater than 2 and 1.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: What about [1, 2, 1, 3, 5, 6, 4]? Find any peak element.
content.successMessage: Excellent! You might have found 2 (greater than 1 and 1) or 6 (greater than 5 and 4).

content.body: You scanned the array from left to right, checking each element against its neighbors. This works, but for large arrays, we can do better by remembering what we've seen.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When arrays have thousands of elements, checking every position becomes inefficient. We need a smarter approach that remembers information as we go. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Think of it like hiking with a notebook. As you climb, you write down the highest point you've seen so far. When you reach a new spot, you check your notebook instead of looking back at every previous location.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll traverse the array once, using a simple comparison to track potential peaks. The key insight: if an element is greater than its next neighbor, it might be a peak - we just need to check the previous neighbor too.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample: Using [1, 2, 3, 1]: Start at 1 → 2 is bigger, move right. At 2 → 3 is bigger, move right. At 3 → 1 is smaller, check left neighbor (2): 3 > 2, so 3 is a peak. We found it in one pass!

content.body:
1. Start from the first element
2. Compare current element with next neighbor
3. If current is greater, check previous neighbor
4. If it's also greater (or doesn't exist), we found a peak
5. Otherwise, continue to next element
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the function
steps.instruction: Start by creating a function called findPeakElement that takes an array nums as parameter.
steps.hint: Use the function keyword or arrow syntax
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great start! You've created the function skeleton.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Make sure you're defining a function that takes nums as parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's create a function: function findPeakElement(nums) {}

steps.title: Handle edge cases
steps.instruction: First, handle simple cases: if the array has only one element, that's automatically a peak. Return 0 (the index).
steps.hint: Check nums.length and return early if it's 1
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! A single element is always a peak.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close! Check if nums.length === 1 and return 0.

steps.title: Check first element
steps.instruction: Before the loop, check if the first element is a peak by comparing it with the second element. If nums[0] > nums[1], return 0.
steps.hint: Add another if statement after the first check
steps.expectedOutcome: Check first element as potential peak
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Compare nums[0] and nums[1], return 0 if nums[0] is greater.

steps.title: Loop through middle elements
steps.instruction: Now create a loop from i = 1 to nums.length - 2. Inside, check if nums[i] is greater than both neighbors. If true, return i. After the loop, return the last index (nums.length - 1) since we haven't found a peak earlier.
steps.hint: Use a for loop and check nums[i] > nums[i-1] && nums[i] > nums[i+1]
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Add the loop and the final return statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add: for (let i = 1; i < nums.length - 1; i++) { if (nums[i] > nums[i-1] && nums[i] > nums[i+1]) return i; } return nums.length - 1;

content.body: Congratulations! You've learned how to find peak elements efficiently. Remember: the key insight is comparing each element with its neighbors in a single pass. This 'remember what we've seen' approach avoids unnecessary re-scanning and works for arrays of any size.
content.title: Done
